title: Why Death Rites Vary
description: Hertz's double burial, thresholds and pollution, and what graves can tell archaeologists

concepts.title: Hertz and the Double Burial
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1907 the French sociologist Robert Hertz, a student of Émile Durkheim, published "A Contribution to the Study of the Collective Representation of Death" in L'Année sociologique. He didn't do any fieldwork. Working from missionary and colonial reports, he took as his central case the Ngaju Dayak of southern Borneo. They held a first funeral soon after a death. Months or years later came a great second ceremony, the tiwah, at which the bones were cleaned and moved to a permanent ossuary.

Hertz saw a three-way parallel in the long intermediate period between the two rites. The corpse is decomposing and is treated as dangerous. The soul is believed to linger near the living, homeless and possibly vengeful. The mourners are set apart, bound by restrictions on food, dress and work. When only dry bones remain, all three transitions end together. The bones go to their final place, the soul is escorted to the land of the dead, and the mourners return to ordinary life.

His larger claim was that a death takes time to complete socially. A community has to undo a person's place in it gradually, and the visible change of the body gives that work a timetable. He suggested that even single burials often keep a trace of the pattern in a fixed mourning period.

Hertz was killed leading an attack at Marchéville, in northeastern France, in April 1915. His essay reached English readers in 1960 in Death and the Right Hand, translated by Rodney and Claudia Needham.1 Peter Metcalf and Richard Huntington's Celebrations of Death (1979) built on it, drawing on Metcalf's fieldwork among the Berawan, also in Borneo.

concepts.title: Thresholds and Pollution
concepts.contentHtml:
Two years after Hertz, Arnold van Gennep's Les Rites de passage (1909) laid out the three phases of separation, transition and incorporation (covered in the Religious Studies topic). He noted that funerals don't fit the scheme neatly. One might expect rites of separation to dominate, yet in many societies the transitional phase is the longest and most elaborate. The dead spend a long time in between, and the living wait with them.

A second recurring theme is pollution. In Purity and Danger (1966) the anthropologist Mary Douglas argued that dirt is "matter out of place," so what a society treats as polluting reveals how it classifies the world.1 A corpse is the great anomaly, a person who has become a thing, and the rules about it often concern order, with hygiene secondary.

The rules differ widely. In the Hebrew Bible (Numbers 19), touching a corpse makes a person impure for seven days, removed with water mixed with the ashes of a red heifer, and men of priestly descent (kohanim) still avoid cemeteries. In Hindu practice the family observes a period of death impurity, commonly 10 to 13 days, while rites help the departed become an ancestor. Islamic law requires washing, shrouding and burial as soon as possible, often within a day, and forbids cremation. Zoroastrians, as the next lesson shows, judge the corpse so polluting that it mustn't touch earth, fire or water.

Maurice Bloch and Jonathan Parry's Death and the Regeneration of Life (1982) added a third theme. Many rites use death to renew fertility and the continuity of the group.

concepts.title: What Graves Can and Cannot Tell
concepts.contentHtml:
Dig up a grave and you meet death rites only through what's left: bones, graves and objects. Around 1970 Arthur Saxe and Lewis Binford argued that the elaboration of a burial tracks the dead person's social standing, so cemeteries could be read as maps of rank. Peter Ucko (1969) had already used ethnographic cases to warn that one burial form can mean very different things. Mike Parker Pearson later put the problem simply. The dead do not bury themselves. A grave records what the mourners chose to say.

Some questions bones now answer well. Skeletons show age, sex, disease and injury. Carbon and nitrogen isotopes indicate diet, and strontium and oxygen isotopes in tooth enamel suggest where a person grew up. Ancient DNA reveals kinship. A 2021 study of the Hazleton North long cairn in Gloucestershire, England, built around 3700 BCE, identified 27 close relatives spanning five generations.1 Sorted, disarticulated or plastered bones, like the plastered skulls from Neolithic Jericho, show that remains were handled long after death. That's the archaeological signature of secondary rites.

Other questions stay out of reach. Belief can't be excavated, and a sword in a grave might mark status, serve the dead in an afterlife or remove a dangerous object from circulation. Practices that leave no grave, such as exposure, scattering or disposal in rivers, are nearly invisible, which is one reason archaeologists suspect that most people in parts of Iron Age Britain were treated in ways that left no burial. Celebrated finds can also be reread. The "flower burial" proposed for a Neanderthal at Shanidar Cave rested on pollen that many researchers now attribute to burrowing rodents or nesting bees, though the debate continues.

title: Towers of Silence
description: Zoroastrian exposure, the Parsis of Mumbai and the collapse of South Asia's vultures

concepts.title: The Purity Logic of Exposure
concepts.contentHtml:
Zoroastrianism, the ancient religion of Iran, sees the world as a contest between the good creation of Ahura Mazda and the destructive work of the Hostile Spirit, Angra Mainyu. Death belongs to the second. In the Videvdad (often spelled Vendidad), the Avesta's priestly law code, a corpse is seized at death by the demon of decay, Nasu, and becomes the strongest source of pollution there is. Earth, water and fire are sacred creations, so burial, river disposal and cremation would all defile them.

The answer was exposure. The Videvdad prescribes laying the dead on high ground, away from water and plants, within reach of dogs and carrion birds, and later gathering the dry bones into an ossuary (astodan). Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BCE, reported that the Magi left their dead to be torn by birds or dogs, and that Persians coated corpses in wax before burying them. Practice was clearly mixed.

The purpose-built tower, the dakhma, is documented only from about the ninth century CE. It is a round, raised stone platform inside a high wall, open to the sky, with three concentric rings of shallow stone beds: men on the outer ring, women in the middle, children nearest the center. The dry bones are later swept into a central pit. "Tower of Silence" is an English name from the colonial period.

A dog is brought to look at the corpse, the sagdid or "dog's gaze," believed to drive back the Nasu.1 Only trained corpse bearers enter the tower; mourners stay outside. Prayers continue for the soul, which Zoroastrians believe is judged at the Chinvat Bridge at dawn on the fourth day after death.

concepts.title: Doongerwadi and the Parsis
concepts.contentHtml:
After the Arab conquest of Iran in the seventh century, Zoroastrians there slowly became a minority. Some migrated to Gujarat in western India, where their descendants are known as Parsis ("Persians"). A tradition recorded in the Qissa-i Sanjan (1599) describes their landing, which scholars date anywhere from the eighth to the tenth century CE. Parsis prospered in Bombay (now Mumbai) as merchants and later industrialists, and the city's first dakhma was built in the 1670s. Its towers stand in Doongerwadi, a walled, wooded estate on Malabar Hill.

In Iran exposure faded during the twentieth century. As cities grew toward the towers, Zoroastrians in Tehran, Kerman and Yazd turned to cemeteries where graves are lined with stone or cement so that the body does not touch the earth. Accounts differ on when the last towers near Yazd stopped receiving bodies, with dates given from the 1960s to 1974.

In Mumbai the towers stayed in use and became a marker of identity for a shrinking community: India's census counted about 57,000 Parsis in 2011, against more than 100,000 in the 1940s. The Bombay Parsi Punchayet, which manages Doongerwadi, and most senior priests hold that consigning the body to the tower, dokhmenashini, is the only proper method. Reformists reply that the method depends on birds the city no longer has.

Priests who performed prayers for cremated Parsis have faced bans from officiating at Doongerwadi. In 2015 a prayer hall opened beside the municipal crematorium at Worli, giving families who choose cremation a place for Zoroastrian rites. Press reports a few years later suggested that about one Parsi funeral in ten in the city ended in cremation.

concepts.title: When the Vultures Vanished
concepts.contentHtml:
A dakhma depends on vultures. A flock of griffon vultures can strip a body within hours; without them, decomposition in Mumbai's humid climate takes weeks or longer. From the 1990s South Asia's vultures died in enormous numbers. Three Gyps species, the white-rumped, Indian and slender-billed vultures, fell by more than 95 percent in about fifteen years, the white-rumped vulture by more than 99 percent, among the fastest declines recorded for any bird.

The cause was identified in 2004, when a team led by J. Lindsay Oaks reported in Nature that vultures in Pakistan were dying of kidney failure after feeding on the carcasses of cattle treated with diclofenac, a cheap anti-inflammatory painkiller. India, Nepal and Pakistan banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006, and in 2023 India also banned two related drugs, ketoprofen and aceclofenac. A safer drug, meloxicam, is promoted instead, and captive-breeding centers have begun releasing birds, but numbers remain far below their former levels.

The loss reached well beyond the Parsis. Uneaten carcasses fed feral dogs and rats, and a 2024 economic study estimated that the collapse contributed to roughly half a million additional human deaths in India between 2000 and 2005, through rabies and contaminated water; the figure is a statistical estimate, not a count.

At Doongerwadi the trustees installed solar concentrators, large mirrors that focus sunlight on the bodies to speed drying. They work on clear days but do little during the monsoon, and they handle only a few bodies at a time. Proposals to breed vultures in an aviary on the estate have been discussed since the 2000s.

title: Sky Burial in Tibet
description: Jhator, the body breakers, Buddhist reasoning and the politics of watching

concepts.title: Giving Alms to the Birds
concepts.contentHtml:
In Tibetan the rite is jhator (written bya gtor), "scattered for the birds," often described as giving alms to the birds; "sky burial" is a Western phrase. For many Tibetans on the central and western plateau it remains the usual way of treating the dead, and it is also practiced in Tibetan Buddhist areas of Nepal, such as Upper Mustang, and in Tibetan regions of Qinghai and Sichuan.

The rite begins before the body leaves home. Lamas recite texts to guide the consciousness through the bardo, the intermediate state between death and rebirth, which tradition says can last up to 49 days. The body is usually kept for a few days while prayers are said, and an astrologer may choose the day. Before dawn it is carried to a charnel ground (durtro).

There the rogyapa, the "body breakers," prepare the corpse so that vultures, chiefly Himalayan griffons, can consume it entirely; the bones are crushed and mixed with roasted barley flour (tsampa) so that nothing is left. Rogyapa have often been of low social status, and observers have described them talking and laughing as they work. Relatives may watch from a distance or stay away.

The Buddhist reasoning is that the consciousness has already left, so the body is an empty vessel. Giving it to the birds is a last act of generosity (dana) toward other living beings, and a lesson in impermanence for those who remain. Some Tibetans speak of the vultures as dakini, sky-going female beings. If the birds leave part of the body, it is traditionally read as a bad sign about the dead person's karma.

concepts.title: Ecology and Origins
concepts.contentHtml:
Geography helps explain the rite. Much of the Tibetan Plateau lies above the tree line, so wood for cremation is scarce and costly, and the ground is often rocky or frozen, which makes digging graves hard. Vultures, by contrast, are plentiful. Ecology does not explain everything, though: Tibetans have long used several methods, assigned partly by status and by cause of death.

High lamas and some dignitaries were traditionally cremated, and the most revered teachers were embalmed and enshrined in stupas; the tombs of several Dalai Lamas stand inside the Potala Palace in Lhasa. In many areas earth burial was reserved for people who died of contagious disease, and sometimes for criminals, and was considered inauspicious. In some regions bodies, especially of the poor or of small children, were given to rivers.

When jhator began is uncertain. The emperors of Tibet's imperial period (seventh to ninth centuries) were buried in great earthen mounds at Chongye, southeast of Lhasa. In a 1996 study the Tibetologist Dan Martin found no clear reference to sky burial in imperial-era or early medieval Tibetan sources. Possible allusions appear in twelfth-century religious biographies, and the first outside description comes from the Franciscan friar Odoric of Pordenone in the early fourteenth century, an account Martin judged unreliable in its details.

Martin offered two hypotheses, both explicitly unproven. One links the rite's spread to Chöd ("cutting"), a meditation in which practitioners visualize offering their own bodies to demons, associated with the Indian teacher Padampa Sangye (died 1117) and the Tibetan yogini Machik Labdrön; Chöd practitioners often presided at charnel grounds. The other, which he thought "rather likely," is that exposure reached Tibet through contact with Zoroastrian Central Asia.

concepts.title: Regulation and the Tourist Gaze
concepts.contentHtml:
After the People's Liberation Army entered Tibet in 1950, and especially during the Cultural Revolution (1966 to 1976), sky burial was attacked as superstition and suppressed in many places. It continued quietly in the countryside and returned openly after the reforms of the late 1970s and 1980s. Since then the state has treated it as an ethnic custom to be protected and managed.

According to Chinese state media, the Tibet Autonomous Region issued provisional rules from 1985 onward, and regulations in 2005 banned photographing or filming the ceremony and reporting it in the media; in 2015 state media reported that these protections had been turned into law, including a ban on strangers watching. Vultures are protected under Chinese wildlife law, and some local rules exclude people who died of infectious disease or poisoning from sky burial.

Tourism is the sharpest issue. Official figures show visitors to the Tibet Autonomous Region rising from about 2 million in 2006 to more than 20 million in 2014, and some charnel grounds drew onlookers with cameras. The site near the Larung Gar Buddhist academy in Sertar, Sichuan, outside the autonomous region and its rules, became known as a place where tourists could watch; in 2010 a lama rebuilt its platform and added a parking area for visitors.

Tibetans have long objected to being watched. The rite is a family's farewell, and many believe that noise, cameras or strangers can disturb the departing consciousness. Responsible travel guidance says not to attend unless invited by the family, and never to photograph; critics of "dark tourism" argue that even a respectful audience turns a private rite into a spectacle.

title: Living With the Dead in Tana Toraja
description: The 'sick' dead at home, buffalo funerals, cliff graves, tau tau and ma'nene

concepts.title: The Sick Person in the House
concepts.contentHtml:
The Toraja live in the mountains of South Sulawesi, Indonesia, in the regencies of Tana Toraja and North Toraja.1 Their ancestral houses, tongkonan, have great curved roofs often likened to boats or buffalo horns. The indigenous religion, Aluk To Dolo ("way of the ancestors"), divides rites into rambu tuka' ("rising smoke"), for life and fertility, and rambu solo' ("descending smoke"), for the dead.

Dutch colonial rule reached the highlands early in the twentieth century, and Protestant missions followed. Official figures now count about 86 percent of Toraja as Christian, about 8 percent as Muslim and about 6 percent as followers of Aluk To Dolo, which the Indonesian state classified in 1969 as a branch of Hinduism, since it recognizes only a few religions. Christian Toraja still hold the great funerals.

A death does not lead straight to a funeral. The body is preserved, traditionally with plant preparations and now usually with formalin injections, and kept in the family house, sometimes for months or years. During this time the person is called to makula', usually translated "sick person" and also glossed "the one who is warm." Relatives bring meals and drinks and talk to the body. The person becomes to mate, "dead," only when the funeral rites begin.

The wait has practical reasons: a family needs time to raise money and to gather relatives who have migrated across Indonesia and abroad. But participants also describe it as a relationship, a gradual parting in which the dead remain part of the household. The soul is thought to stay near the village until the funeral is complete and only then to set out for Puya, the land of souls.

concepts.title: Buffalo, Debt and the Funeral Feast
concepts.contentHtml:
A high-status Toraja funeral can last several days and draw thousands of guests. Families build temporary bamboo pavilions around a field, receive delegations in procession, and perform the ma'badong, a slow circle dance with chanted laments for the dead.

At the center is the slaughter of water buffalo (tedong), believed to help the soul reach Puya; more buffalo mean a swifter journey and a higher standing for the family. Elite funerals may see tens of buffalo and hundreds of pigs killed. The most prized animal is the tedong bonga, a piebald buffalo with patches of pink and black, which can cost many times the price of an ordinary animal. The meat is then distributed according to rank.

The feast runs on obligation. Guests bring buffalo, pigs and other gifts that are recorded, and the receiving family is expected to return them in kind at future funerals, so debts pass between households and across generations. In Feasts of Honor (1985) the anthropologist Toby Alice Volkman described how money earned by migrants let families of lower rank stage grand funerals, raising the stakes of status competition. Colonial and Indonesian officials have at times called the spending wasteful and tried to limit or tax it.

Since the 1970s funerals have also been tourist events. About 50 European tourists visited in 1971 and roughly 12,000 in 1976; in 1984 Indonesia's tourism ministry called Tana Toraja the "prima donna" of South Sulawesi. Kathleen Adams's Art as Politics (2006) traces how that attention reshaped the way Toraja present themselves.

concepts.title: Cliff Graves, Tau Tau and Ma'nene
concepts.contentHtml:
After the funeral the body joins the family grave. Wealthy families have chambers cut into cliff faces, as at Lemo; others use natural caves, as at Londa, where old coffins and bones lie in the rock. Some older wooden coffins hang from cliffs. Babies who died before their teeth came in were traditionally placed in a hollow cut into a living tree, a practice associated with the village of Kambira.

High-ranking dead are represented by tau tau, carved wooden effigies set in galleries on the cliff face, looking out over the valley. Older figures are stylized; modern ones are often realistic portraits dressed in real clothes. In the 1980s many were stolen and sold to collectors and museums abroad. Families responded by hiding effigies or fencing their graves.

The best-known rite after burial is ma'nene, held in parts of North Toraja, notably the Pangala' and Baruppu' areas. In August, after the rice harvest, families open their grave houses (patane), clean the remains, repair or replace coffins, and dress the long dead in fresh clothes, sometimes standing them up for a family photograph. How often it happens varies by village, from every year to every few years.

Ma'nene is a local custom, not a pan-Toraja one, and it became known worldwide through photographs in the 2010s. Local tradition tells of a hunter who found an abandoned corpse in the forest, dressed and buried it, and was rewarded with good fortune; that is an origin story, not history. Christians take part as well as Aluk followers, and participants describe the rite as care for relatives, not fear of them.

title: Famadihana in Madagascar
description: Turning the bones: rewrapping the ancestors, tombs and kinship, and modern debates

concepts.title: Rewrapping the Ancestors
concepts.contentHtml:
Famadihana, literally "turning" and usually rendered "the turning of the bones," is practiced mainly by the Merina and Betsileo of Madagascar's central highlands.1 In the dry, cool season, roughly June to September, a family opens its tomb, brings out the bodies of its dead, rewraps them in new shrouds and returns them. A tomb is typically opened every five to seven years, or when an astrologer (mpanandro) advises it or a dead relative appears in a dream asking for new clothes.

The day is festive. Relatives travel from across the country, a band plays, rum is drunk and a zebu may be slaughtered for the feast. The bodies, still in their old shrouds, are carried out on mats, held in laps and arms, spoken to and introduced to children born since the last opening. They are then wrapped in new shrouds called lamba mena. Despite the name, "red cloth," these are often not red, but they are of silk, which makes them costly. Each person's name may be written on the shroud, and the bodies are carried in a dance around the tomb before being laid back inside.

Participants generally describe famadihana as a joyful family occasion. The dead, the razana or ancestors, are a source of blessing (tsodrano) and moral authority, and caring for them holds the living family together. The rite also moves bodies: people who died far away or were placed in temporary graves are brought into the ancestral tomb.

concepts.title: Tombs, Kinship and History
concepts.contentHtml:
The anthropologist Maurice Bloch, who worked among the Merina in the 1960s, explained the rite through the tomb. In Placing the Dead (1971) he showed that Merina identity is anchored in an ancestral land (tanindrazana) and above all in its family tomb (fasana), even for people who live and work elsewhere. Tombs are often built of stone or concrete and cost more than houses: the house is temporary, the tomb permanent.

Bloch argued that repeated rewrapping gradually dissolves each dead person's individuality. As the bodies dry and crumble they are wrapped together and merge into a collective ancestral body, so the rite turns separate deaths into the unity of the descent group. On this reading famadihana is less about individuals than about the group the tomb defines.

Its history is debated. Some scholars think its present form is fairly recent, perhaps no earlier than the seventeenth century, and it probably grew in importance in the nineteenth century, as the Merina kingdom became a major state and stone tombs spread. Others look much further back. Malagasy is an Austronesian language whose closest relatives are the Barito languages of southern Borneo, including Ma'anyan, a link the linguist Otto Christian Dahl demonstrated in 1951. Barito-speaking peoples of Borneo, among them the Ngaju studied by Hertz, practice secondary burial, so some see famadihana as a distant descendant of that tradition.

Skeptics answer that more than a thousand years of local history, African as well as Asian ancestry, and royal politics separate the two, and that secondary burial has arisen independently in many parts of the world.

concepts.title: Cost, Churches and Plague
concepts.contentHtml:
Famadihana is expensive. Silk shrouds, food and drink for hundreds of guests, music and animals can consume a large share of a family's yearly income in one of the world's poorest countries, and families may save for years. Some Malagasy, especially in towns, criticize the expense, and journalists have reported the practice declining in places for that reason, though it remains widespread in the highlands.

Most highland Malagasy are Christian, and the churches disagree about the rite. Protestant missionaries of the London Missionary Society, active from 1818, discouraged ancestral rites. The Catholic Church in Madagascar now accepts famadihana as a cultural commemoration of the dead rather than worship, and many families include Christian prayers. Some evangelical and Pentecostal churches reject it as ancestor worship, and their members have abandoned it in growing numbers.

Health officials worry about disease. Madagascar reports more human plague cases than any other country, usually a few hundred a year. In 2017 an unusual urban outbreak, mostly of pneumonic plague, caused about 2,400 recorded cases and more than 200 deaths between August and November, according to the World Health Organization. Authorities told families that plague victims must not be placed in family tombs that would later be reopened, and warned against exhuming them; some families ignored the warnings.

How much famadihana actually spreads plague is uncertain. Experts disagree about how long the bacterium survives in buried remains; the clearest risk comes from handling the bodies of people who died of pneumonic plague recently. Some researchers stress that rats, fleas, poverty and weak health services drive outbreaks, and that singling out the rite risks stigmatizing a central custom.

title: Ossuaries, Altars and Compost
description: Bone chapels, the many histories of the Day of the Dead, and new ways back into the earth

concepts.title: Bone Chapels and Capuchin Crypts
concepts.contentHtml:
European churchyards were reused for centuries. When graves were dug again, older bones went to charnel houses or ossuaries, and in some Catholic regions they were arranged for display as a memento mori, a reminder of death. In Rome, the crypt beneath the Capuchin church of Santa Maria della Concezione holds the bones of about 3,700 people believed to be friars. The friars brought some 300 cartloads of remains from their old friary in 1631, and the bones were later arranged into arches, rosettes and light fittings across small chapels. A placard reads: "What you are now, we used to be; what we are now, you will be."

At Sedlec, near Kutná Hora in the Czech Republic, the cemetery became desirable after the Cistercian abbot Henry, sent to the Holy Land by King Ottokar II of Bohemia in 1278, sprinkled it with earth from Golgotha. The Black Death and the Hussite Wars filled it. In 1870 the woodcarver František Rint, hired by the Schwarzenberg family, arranged the bones of an estimated 40,000 to 70,000 people into the present display, including a chandelier said to contain every bone of the human body.

In Palermo, Sicily, the Capuchins began in 1599 by preserving a friar, Silvestro of Gubbio. Bodies were dried on racks of ceramic pipes and sometimes washed with vinegar, then dressed and displayed, and local notables later paid to join the friars. The last friar was interred in 1871 and the catacombs officially closed in 1880, but burials continued into the 1920s and 1930s. The best-known body is Rosalia Lombardo, not yet two years old, embalmed by Alfredo Salafia in 1920. A 2011 survey counted 1,252 mummified bodies.

concepts.title: The Day of the Dead and Its Histories
concepts.contentHtml:
Día de Muertos falls on November 1 and 2, the Catholic feasts of All Saints and All Souls; often the first day for dead children and the second for adults. Families build ofrendas, home altars with photographs, candles, orange marigolds (cempasúchil), pan de muerto, sugar skulls and the dead person's favorite food and drink, since the dead are believed to return to visit. In many towns relatives decorate graves and keep night vigils.

The popular story calls it an Aztec festival in Catholic dress. Spanish friars did record that the Mexica devoted two months of their calendar to the dead, but continuity is disputed. The historian Elsa Malvido argued that the feast derives essentially from Spanish All Souls customs and that its status as a national emblem owes much to twentieth-century cultural policy. Octavio Paz, in The Labyrinth of Solitude (1950), saw in it a Mexican intimacy with death. Anthropologists such as Stanley Brandes (2006) describe a colonial hybrid whose strands cannot be cleanly separated.

Its signature image is modern too. José Guadalupe Posada's print of a skeleton in a grand feathered hat, a satire on Mexicans who aped European fashion, dates from around 1910 to 1913. Diego Rivera placed her at the center of his mural Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Park (1946 to 1947), and as La Catrina she became a national icon.

The newest custom came from a film. The James Bond film Spectre (2015) opens with a vast costumed Day of the Dead parade through central Mexico City, though no such parade existed. The city staged one on October 29, 2016, and it has since become a regular event.

concepts.title: Green Burial, Water and Compost
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern Western funerals settled into two defaults: embalming and a sealed coffin, in the US often inside a concrete vault, or cremation. Cremation has spread fast; in the United States it overtook burial in the mid-2010s, and in Japan nearly everyone is cremated. Critics point to embalming chemicals, buried hardwood and metal, and the fuel burned by crematoria.

Natural burial returns to older practice: no embalming, a biodegradable coffin or shroud, no vault, and often a tree or meadow instead of a headstone. Traditional Jewish and Muslim burial has long followed similar rules. The first British woodland burial ground opened at Carlisle Cemetery in 1993, and the UK now has nearly 300 natural burial grounds; in the US, Ramsey Creek Preserve in South Carolina opened in 1998.

Two newer methods change the process itself. Alkaline hydrolysis, marketed as aquamation, dissolves soft tissue in heated water and alkali, leaving bones that are reduced to powder; Archbishop Desmond Tutu's body was treated this way in 2022, at his request. Human composting, legally "natural organic reduction," keeps the body in a vessel with wood chips, straw and alfalfa for several weeks until it becomes soil. Washington became the first US state to legalize it, in 2019, and Katrina Spade's company Recompose began operating there soon after. By 2025 more than a dozen states had followed.

Religious responses vary. In 2023 the doctrine committee of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops judged that composting and alkaline hydrolysis do not show the respect owed to the body, and Catholic groups have lobbied against legalization in several states. Supporters, including some clergy, present the new methods as a literal form of "dust to dust."
